actionThatDiffers: Triage which blocked pane to service first, and pre-form the answer, instead of visiting each pane to discover which question is cheap; the trip still happens, only better ordered.
why: The blocking question is literally printed in the session pane, so a tmux list-panes + capture-pane loop yields an adequate approximation of what each one wants (rule 2 caps at 60); the residual work is enumerating panes, so mid-40s. Impact is real but bounded: knowing the question does not answer it, and Claude Desktop already dots the sessions needing input, so vendors are visibly walking toward the needs-input half. Extracting *what* it wants from a transcript is a heuristic, hence detector-dependent.

actionThatDiffers: Jump straight into the right pane instead of cycling tabs to find it — same destination, a few seconds sooner.
why: Rule 5: this is a thing the user DOES. Today it is cmd+N, a tab click, or tmux select-window -t — one command in a place the user knows, so 30. Impact is pure convenience: nothing about the decision changes, only the seconds spent navigating. With 12 unlabelled tabs the hunt is annoying, but annoyance is not delta (rule 1), so it stays in the minor-convenience band.

actionThatDiffers: Go merge, close, or delete a specific branch/PR you had forgotten, instead of letting it rot — but only for the branch half, since GitHub already nags you about open PRs.
why: gh search prs --author @me --state open covers the PR half org-wide in one command, and git branch --no-merged covers branches with a per-repo loop — an adequate approximation, so rule 2/3 territory, low-50s for the correlation cost. Impact discounted hard: GitHub's own dashboard, email, and PR list are the commodity here and a forgotten local branch usually costs nothing. Attributing a leftover branch to an ended session is a heuristic.

actionThatDiffers: After a break, skip re-reading five scrollbacks and open only the one session the digest flags — saves reading minutes, but the decision about what to do next is unchanged.
why: A digest is not reachable by hand: capture-pane -S gives you the raw scrollback, which is precisely the reading you were trying to avoid, and it spans sessions and time. No tool computes it, so access is genuinely high. But the actionable slice of re-entry — who is blocked, who is stale — is already carried by the state badges, so D10's marginal delta is narrative recap, and a cautious user re-reads the important session anyway. Summary quality rests entirely on a heuristic.

actionThatDiffers: Notice a hosted/cowork session that needs you from the same board as local ones, rather than remembering to check the vendor web tab — one fewer surface to poll.
why: Hosted and cowork sessions live in a vendor web UI that shows them unprompted and emails/notifies on completion — that is one click in a place the user already knows, so access is low-30s; merging two visible surfaces is a union, which rule 3 keeps capped. Commodity risk is the highest on the board: this is the vendors' own product surface and they ship inbox views for it, so a third-party mirror is a year from being redundant. Impact is convenience, not a changed decision.

actionThatDiffers: none — the item's own stated outcome is "no decision attached"; at most you eventually run an upgrade command you would have run anyway.
why: claude --version / codex --version is one command per harness in the place the user knows to look, and harnesses nag about their own updates, so 30. Impact is near-floor by rule 1: no concrete action differs. Version drift surfaces itself the moment something breaks, and health is a word doing no work here. This is inventory decoration, not a decision input.

actionThatDiffers: Service a blocked session on your other machine that would otherwise sit stalled overnight; for the team variant, nothing you do changes — you watch someone else's work.
why: Sessions on another host are genuinely out of reach by hand — no local pane loop crosses machines, and a teammate's sessions are invisible in principle — so access is near the top. The data is absent locally rather than heuristic, hence no detector dependency. Impact is where it collapses: the team framing is a manager dashboard with real privacy friction and no action for the developer, the multi-machine framing is real but a minority setup, and both demand the user stand up shared infrastructure first, which is a heavy adoption toll on a mild payoff.

actionThatDiffers: Close or resume a session that has gone quiet — but doing nothing about a quiet session usually costs nothing, so the action is often just tidying.
why: tmux exposes a last-activity epoch per window, and transcript file mtime works too, so a six-line loop plus a 2h comparison is an adequate approximation — rule 2 and rule 3 both bite, mid-40s. Judged as if unshipped (rule 6): a 2h threshold on a visible timestamp is arithmetic. Impact is low because most stale sessions are simply finished; the alarming case (an agent that quietly died mid-task) is already caught by the needs-input/no-output signals, and the unharvested-work case belongs to E5.

actionThatDiffers: Decide whether to wait out the current turn or leave and start something else — a micro-decision made dozens of times a day, made on an estimate rather than a guess.
why: The briefing is explicit that no harness estimates turn duration, and no hand method produces one; elapsed time is on screen but the projection is not, so access is high. Rule 4 applies squarely — the number does not exist anywhere, so its worth rests entirely on the estimator being right, and agent turn lengths are heavy-tailed enough that a confident wrong ETA misdirects the very decision it informs. That reliability discount is why impact sits just above the decision threshold rather than in the loss-prevention band: the fallback (go do something else and glance back) is cheap and already what people do.
